sections.title: What is Math for CP?
sections.content:
Competitive programming math problems require recognizing mathematical patterns, applying formulas, and translating problem statements into equations. Unlike number theory (integers and divisibility) or combinatorics (structured counting), 'math for CP' is a grab-bag of techniques: arithmetic and geometric series sums, floor/ceiling manipulation, coordinate transformations, and pattern-finding.

The key skill is **pattern recognition** — noticing that a problem's answer follows a simple closed-form formula, or that a counting problem reduces to a known mathematical identity. Many CP problems that look like they require iteration have O(1) or O(√n) solutions.

These techniques appear as standalone problems ('count multiples in range', 'sum of all subarray elements') and as subroutines inside larger algorithms. Knowing the standard formulas cold prevents you from wasting time deriving them under pressure.

Before reaching for a loop, ask: does this quantity have a closed form? If you are summing an arithmetic or geometric sequence, computing a count of multiples, or measuring grid distances, there is likely a formula.

sections.title: When to Use This
sections.content: Apply CP math when the problem asks for a sum, count, or aggregate with arithmetic structure — sums over ranges, counts of multiples, contributions of elements to all subarrays. Also when geometric distances can be simplified by a coordinate transformation.

sections.title: Series Sums, Floor Arithmetic, Pigeonhole, and Coordinate Tricks
sections.content:
## Series and Sums

- Sum 1 to n: `n*(n+1)/2`
- Sum of squares 1² to n²: `n*(n+1)*(2n+1)/6`
- Sum of cubes: `[n*(n+1)/2]²`
- Geometric: `a*(r^n-1)/(r-1)` for r≠1

**Subarray contribution**: `arr[i]` appears in `(i+1)*(n-i)` subarrays of length-n array. Total sum of all subarray sums = `sum of arr[i]*(i+1)*(n-i)`. Converts O(n²) to O(n).

## Floor/Ceiling Arithmetic

- Multiples of k in [1,n]: `Math.floor(n/k)`
- Multiples of k in [l,r]: `Math.floor(r/k) - Math.floor((l-1)/k)`
- Integer ceiling of n/k: `Math.floor((n+k-1)/k)`

## Pigeonhole Principle

If n items go into m containers and n > m, at least one container holds ≥ 2 items. Proves existence: given n+1 integers from [1,n], two must be equal. Used to bound solutions and prove collision inevitability.

## Coordinate Rotation for L∞ Distance

Transform `(x,y)` → `(x+y, x-y)`. Under this transformation, Chebyshev distance (max of |dx|, |dy|) relates simply to axis-aligned ranges in the new coordinates. Finding max Chebyshev distance = finding max range of u coordinates and max range of v coordinates independently.

## Pattern-Finding

Bulb switcher: bulb k is toggled once per divisor of k; ends on iff it has an odd number of divisors; only perfect squares have odd divisors. Answer = floor(sqrt(n)). Recognize exhaustive simulation has a mathematical answer.

sections.title: Sieve-Based Multiplicative Function Computation
sections.content:
The Sieve of Eratosthenes (covered in Number Theory) finds all primes up to N in O(N log log N) - but the same sieving idea extends to computing an entire ARRAY of number-theoretic values for every integer up to N in one pass, instead of computing each one individually.

**Smallest Prime Factor (SPF) sieve**: instead of just marking composites, store the smallest prime factor that marked each composite number. Once built, ANY number's full prime factorization can be extracted in O(log n) by repeatedly dividing by its SPF - turning what would be O(sqrt(n)) per-number factorization into O(log n) per number after one shared O(n log log n) preprocessing pass, a big win when factorizing many numbers rather than just one.

**Euler's Totient sieve**: compute `phi(i)` (count of numbers <= i coprime to i) for every `i` up to N simultaneously, using the multiplicative property `phi(p^k) = p^k - p^(k-1)` for each prime factor discovered during sieving, combined via `phi(n) = n * product over distinct prime factors p of (1 - 1/p)`. This answers 'give me phi(i) for every i up to N' in one O(N log log N) pass, instead of N separate O(sqrt(i)) computations.

The shared pattern across both: whenever a problem needs a number-theoretic property (factorization, totient, divisor count) for EVERY number up to some bound N, rather than just one number, a sieve-based precomputation is almost always faster than computing each one independently - the same 'batch the shared work' idea that motivates plain prefix sums, just applied to multiplicative number theory instead of addition.

sections.title: Core Template
sections.explanation: Reference implementations of core CP math formulas. subarraySum demonstrates the element-contribution pattern replacing O(n^2) nested loops with O(n). Coordinate rotation converts Chebyshev distance maximization to simple range queries.

items.name: Perfect Square / Divisor Count Problems
items.description: Problems where the answer depends on counting perfect squares or numbers with odd divisor count. Only perfect squares have odd divisors because divisors come in pairs (d and n/d) except when d = sqrt(n).

items.name: Minimum Moves via Mathematical Insight
items.description: Minimum operations problems often reduce to a formula. 'Minimum moves to make all elements equal' = sum of differences from the minimum. Recognizing the mathematical invariant avoids simulation entirely.
items.example_problem: Minimum Moves to Equal Array Elements

items.name: Floor Division Range Counting
items.description: Count integers in a range satisfying a divisibility condition in O(1) using floor division. Generalizes to any modular condition: count multiples of k in [l,r] = floor(r/k) - floor((l-1)/k).
items.example_problem: Count Odd Numbers in an Interval Range

sections.title: Complexity
sections.time: O(1) for closed-form formulas; O(n) for subarray contribution patterns
sections.explanation: Closed-form formulas compute in O(1) regardless of n. Subarray contribution requires one pass: O(n). Coordinate rotation is O(n) to transform all points and find extremes. The power of these techniques is replacing O(n^2) or O(n*k) loops with O(1) or O(n).

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Integer overflow in sum formulas: n*(n+1)/2 overflows 32-bit integers for n > ~65535. In JavaScript safe up to n ≈ 2^26 before floating point precision loss. Use BigInt for very large n.
Integer vs float division: n/k in JavaScript returns a float. Always use Math.floor(n/k) explicitly when you need integer quotient.
Sum of 1 to n vs 0 to n-1: n*(n+1)/2 for 1..n; n*(n-1)/2 for 0..n-1. Off-by-one in the formula produces answers that are close but wrong.

Ceiling formula confusion: Math.ceil(n/k), Math.floor((n+k-1)/k), and Math.floor((n-1)/k)+1 are all equivalent. Pick one and use it consistently — mixing them when n is an exact multiple of k causes subtle bugs.

Coordinate rotation scaling: after rotating (x,y) to (x+y, x-y), distances in the new space are scaled relative to original. When comparing transformed distances to thresholds, verify the scaling factor.

items.title: Count Odd Numbers in an Interval Range
items.why: Floor division range counting — derive the O(1) formula for counting integers satisfying a modular condition without iteration.

items.title: Minimum Moves to Equal Array Elements
items.why: Mathematical invariant — incrementing n-1 elements equals decrementing one, reducing to summing differences from the minimum.

items.title: Bulb Switcher
items.why: Divisor count pattern — answer is count of perfect squares ≤ n, testing whether you derive the mathematical pattern instead of simulating.

items.title: Minimum Number of Steps to Make Two Strings Anagram
items.why: Frequency difference formula — reduce an operations problem to summing excess character frequencies.
